item.title: Stocks Fall and Oil Rises as Investors Retreat from Mounting Risks
item.description:
Global markets shuddered on Thursday as stocks fell after earnings reports from big technology companies spooked investors and oil jumped to its highest level in months on a series of worrisome developments in the conflict in the Middle East.

Strikes in Saudi Arabia and around the Persian Gulf helped drive the price of Brent crude, the global benchmark for oil, up 3 percent to about $112 a barrel, its highest level since May.

West Texas Intermediate crude, the U.S. benchmark, also rose, to nearly $100 a barrel.

Oil had reached as high as $120 a barrel since the start of the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran nearly eight months ago, which has disrupted exports from the energy-rich Persian Gulf region. Before the war, global oil was trading around $70 a barrel and about 20 percent of the world’s oil flowed through the Strait of Hormuz, an artery between Iran and Oman that has become treacherous for commercial ships since the start of the fighting. Oil flows through the strait are running at about 75 percent of prewar levels, according to Kpler, a maritime data company.

In the United States, the average price of gasoline was $4.27 a gallon on Thursday, according to the AAA motor club, up 43 percent since the war began. The average price of diesel has surged 68 percent over that period, to $6.31 per gallon.

Source: FactSet.

The New York Times

Futures on the S&P 500 pointed to a 1 percent decline when stocks resume trading in the United States on Thursday. The tech-heavy Nasdaq was set for a steeper fall, approaching 2 percent.

Large tech companies at the forefront of the A.I. expansion pulled down market indexes, as investors have grown more wary of the returns promised by wildly expensive A.I. projects. On Wednesday after markets closed, Meta reported a big decline in its cash flow and said it would issue a new class of stock to help raise more money to spend on data centers and other A.I. initiatives. Earnings at Tesla fell short of Wall Street expectations, as the automaker run by Elon Musk poured resources into self-driving vehicles, humanoid robots and other new technologies.

Major markets in Asia, which are heavily influenced by technology industry trends, posted declines, with benchmark indexes in Hong Kong, Japan and South Korea all down by at least 2 percent. In Europe, the Stoxx 600, an index that tracks the region’s largest companies, fell about 1 percent.

How stocks are trading in the United States

Source: FactSet.

The New York Times

Violence flared in the Middle East overnight, another factor weighing on markets. At least two people were killed in a strike on an airport in Dammam, Saudi Arabia, the home city of Saudi Aramco, the state oil giant. Two other people died after air defenses intercepted a drone that targeted an oil field run by Aramco. The Saudi government did not say who they believed was responsible for the attacks. The Iranian-backed Houthi militia in Yemen has been striking Saudi infrastructure for weeks.

Saudi Aramco staff were instructed to leave the company’s headquarters building in Dhahran and to work remotely on Thursday, according to two people familiar with the situation who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak for the company. Aramco did not respond to a request for comment and the Saudi energy ministry referred questions to Aramco.

In the Persian Gulf, several commercial ships have been attacked in recent days. On Tuesday night, a tanker carrying oil products, the Soyia, was reportedly struck while at anchor in the northern Persian Gulf, according to Marisks, a maritime risk firm. Another ship, a Kuwait-flagged crude oil tanker, was struck on Wednesday while sailing through the Strait of Hormuz, causing a fire on the ship, according to a maritime agency operated by Pakistan’s Navy.

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps said on Thursday that it had struck four tankers in the northern Persian Gulf that it claimed had been illegally transferring oil. It also said that three more vessels had hit mines in the western Strait of Hormuz. Those attacks could not immediately be independently confirmed.

In an article published in The Financial Times, Abbas Araghchi, Iran’s foreign minister, said that Iran, “simply by virtue of geography, will always have unparalleled leverage over maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz.” He warned that any further escalation from the United States would result in a “painful outcome.”

Jenny Gross and Lisa Friedman contributed reporting from London.

item.title: Monet Painting Sells for $56 Million in France
item.description:
A large Claude Monet painting of flowers in his Giverny water garden sold for 50 million euros (about $56 million) at Sotheby’s in Paris on Thursday.

After a 42-minute bidding tussle between at least six would-be buyers on telephones, the painting, titled “Iris,” was bought by an Asian client bidding by phone with Jen Hua, deputy chairman of Sotheby’s Asia.

“I’ve never seen bidding that long,” said Helly Nahmad, a London dealer who specializes in modern art.

“It was insane,” he added, “but these things are mega-rare.”

The world record for a Monet painting is $110.7 million, set in 2019 at Sotheby’s with the sale of the 1890 painting “Meules,” or “Grainstacks.” (The price would be $145.7 million today, adjusted for inflation.)

“Iris,” which is about 5 feet tall and nearly 6 feet wide, depicts flowers swaying above skies reflected in Monet’s famous lily pond. Experts think the canvas was painted in the open air in 1924-25, toward the end of the artist’s life. It had been estimated to sell for between €20 million to €30 million.

Until recently, owners of high-value artworks routinely consigned their trophies to auctions in either New York or London. But since Brexit has made Britain a less attractive destination for art sales, European collectors have been more willing to sell in Paris.

In March, Alon Zakaim, a London dealer, offered a rare pair of Monet “series” landscape paintings from the 1890s at TEFAF Maastricht, in the Netherlands, with an asking price of $20 million. They found a buyer after the fair.

“It was a pretty painting with a modern look that attracts new buyers,” Zakaim said of the painting sold on Thursday. “It relates well to later 20th-century works,” he added. “The appetite for these large, late Monet paintings is increasing.”

“Iris” had been in the collection of Jeanne Schlumberger, an heiress to the Schlumberger energy company, now known as SLB. During the 1950s and ’60s, with the help of the pioneering Paris dealer Katia Granoff, Schlumberger amassed an extensive collection of Impressionist and modern art, including late paintings by Monet, which were then out of fashion, according to Sotheby’s.

“Iris” was among about 50 Monets that Granoff bought from the artist’s son Michel in 1956. Schlumberger acquired it the following year.

“Once the painting arrived in her house, it left the world,” Thomas Bompard, a senior international specialist at Sotheby’s Paris, said in an interview before the auction. He said the painting had “never been exhibited.”

Schlumberger died in 1983, and her descendants have chosen the 100th anniversary of Monet’s death to sell “Iris” and 26 other works from her collection at Sotheby’s.

Cyrille de Gunzburg, a private dealer in Paris, said in an interview at the Sotheby’s pre-auction view that he had negotiated the sale of a Monet from a similar date for $15 million in 2013.

“Art history tells us that Cézanne was the big influence on Modern art,” he said. “Paintings like this show it was also Monet.”

In recent years, as Monet’s influence on Abstract Expressionism and other 20th-century art movements has been more widely appreciated, wealthy collectors have coveted the artist’s late works.

“This painting could be benchmarked against the great Monets in the museums of Paris,” said Helena Newman, Sotheby’s worldwide chairman of Impressionist & Modern art. “It was a true museum quality work.”

Overall, the Schlumberger collection raised €74.4 million, or about $83.5 million.

item.title: ‘Cats Love Gravy’: How a Reporter Ended Up at a Pet Food Research Center
item.description:
Times Insider explains who we are and what we do and delivers behind-the-scenes insights into how our journalism comes together.

I was sitting at my desk doing one of those things business journalists do, streaming an investor conference, when I heard something that made me giggle.

“We have seen good structural growth in cat,” said Philipp Navratil, the chief executive of Nestlé.

Structural growth in cat? He went on. Many more people were adopting cats than dogs.

“We like cats a lot because cats are also picky eaters,” he said, adding that this worked to Nestlé’s advantage because the company had the scientific resources to understand and cater to the taste buds of cats.

I had a lot of questions.

I was surprised that many more people were choosing cats over dogs. I love dogs. I recently read cover to cover a book called “Be More Dog: Life Lessons From Our Canine Friends,” a gift from a dog-loving friend. But Mr. Navratil’s comments, I learned, were true.

The number of cat-owning households grew at a rate three times as fast as that of dog-owning households from 2021-25, according to a Euromonitor survey. The hypothesis is that people are spending more time in the office these days, and cats are lower maintenance.

Maybe, but cats are decidedly not lower maintenance when it comes to food. Curious about how, exactly, researchers determine which flavors are most appealing to dogs and cats, I set out to explore the business of pet food at a time when people are spending more on their animals and have more options.

I began my reporting in June with a trip to Switzerland to the headquarters of Nestlé, which owns the pet food company Purina. I watched the company present a pyramid-shaped mousse with cascading gravy, part of Purina’s premium food line.

“Cats love gravy,” one Purina employee said, calling the dish “an elevated experience for the cat and cat parent.”

In an interview, Dan Smith, who works in strategy for Purina, told me about the investments the company was making to understand what flavors cats like and even how they bite their food. (Note from Jenny’s editor, a cat guy: Anyone familiar with cats knows they chomp food with their heads at an angle.) People are having fewer children and having them later, if at all, and are willing to spend more money to keep their pets happy.

“I had grand-dogs before I had grandkids,” Mr. Smith said.

I began thinking of the ideal setting for a story about the picky palates of our pets. Should I find the place with the highest number of cats per capita? Turkey? Poland, one of the countries where Nestlé saw the most growth potential? My editor suggested I find out if big pet food companies had special facilities to research animal palates.

I asked around, and Royal Canin, which is owned by Mars, invited me to their pet center, home to 377 cats and dogs, in southern France. This was shaping up to be a dream assignment.

I arrived at Royal Canin’s pet center, near Montpellier, in September. Dozens of small dogs of various breeds were barking and running around outside. One dog watched the others from an elevated training platform, while two others played in the shade. Around the corner, a corgi puppy and three Beaucerons were jumping in and out of a swimming pool. An employee told me the pool was “for dogs, by dogs,” although I didn’t quite know what to make of that.

On a video call, a feline expert explained to me why cats love tuna — it has the perfect combination of the umami flavor profile that cats savor. Only about 40 percent of the dogs and the cats that live at the Royal Canin pet center participate in taste tests, and the rest participate in studies involving their health. The members of the select group have shown they can distinguish between palatable and less palatable food.

Dogs of certain breeds that are less discerning, such as Labradors, don’t make the cut, said Silvia Miret-Catalan, vice president of research and development at Royal Canin. (My partner’s dog, Taya, a Swedish Vallhund mix who has eaten poop on more than one occasion, would almost certainly be ineligible.)

To qualify for Purina’s taste tests, dogs and cats also have to show they have “polite feeding behaviors,” such as not flipping over bowls at mealtimes, in the case of dogs, said Annie Valuska, a pet behaviorist at Purina, which also conducts palatability tests. Experts study the way cats approach a bowl, whether they purr before or while eating and the extent to which they paw, said Catherine Cartier, the research director of Nestlé Purina Europe.

Royal Canin’s dog taste tests last about 15 minutes, but cat taste tests stretch for hours. At the pet center, I observed A/B kibble tests and hoped a serious-looking cat named Virgule (“comma” in French), a Ragdoll cat, would eat some food from either Tray A or Tray B, rather than just stare at me. She just stared.

Experts emphasized that while kibble tests can provide useful conclusions about the preferences of cats of different ages and breeds, no one rule fits all cats.

Or, as one reader put it in a comment after my article published, “can someone tell my cat that he’s supposed to like tuna?”
